questions.stem: A ray of light passes from air into a glass block at an angle to the normal. What happens to the light ray as it enters the glass?

options.text: It speeds up and bends away from the normal
It slows down and bends towards the normal
It slows down and bends away from the normal
It speeds up and bends towards the normal

questions.explanation: Glass is optically denser than air, so light slows down when entering glass. When light enters a denser medium and slows down, it bends towards the normal. Option C has the correct speed change but wrong bending direction. The rule is: slower = towards normal, faster = away from normal.

questions.stem: A swimming pool appears shallower than it actually is when viewed from above. This is because:

options.text: Water absorbs light, making the pool look darker
Light refracts as it leaves the water, bending away from the normal, making the bottom appear closer to the surface
The water acts as a magnifying glass
Light reflects off the surface of the water

questions.explanation: Light from the pool bottom speeds up as it passes from water (denser) to air (less dense), bending away from the normal. Our brain traces the light back in straight lines, making the bottom appear higher up (shallower) than it really is. This is a real-world application of refraction and explains why pools can be dangerously deceptive.

questions.stem: A light ray hits a glass block along the normal (at 0° to the normal). What happens?

options.text: The light bends towards the normal
The light bends away from the normal
The light passes straight through without bending, but slows down
Total internal reflection occurs

questions.explanation: When light hits a boundary along the normal (angle of incidence = 0°), there is no change in direction — it passes straight through. However, the speed still changes (it slows down in glass). Refraction (bending) only occurs when light enters at an angle to the normal. Total internal reflection (option D) only occurs when light tries to leave a denser medium at an angle greater than the critical angle.

questions.stem: Total internal reflection occurs in an optical fibre. Which conditions must both be met for total internal reflection to happen?

options.text: Light must travel from a less dense to a more dense medium, and the angle must be greater than the critical angle
Light must travel from a more dense to a less dense medium, and the angle of incidence must be greater than the critical angle
Light must travel from a more dense to a less dense medium, and the angle of incidence must be less than the critical angle
Light must hit the boundary at exactly the critical angle

questions.explanation: Total internal reflection requires TWO conditions: (1) light must be travelling from a more optically dense medium to a less dense medium (e.g., glass to air), and (2) the angle of incidence must exceed the critical angle. Option A has the wrong direction of travel. Option C has the correct direction but the wrong angle condition. At exactly the critical angle (option D), light travels along the boundary — it does not reflect internally.

questions.stem: When waves in a ripple tank pass from deep water to shallow water at an angle, what happens to the wave speed, frequency, and wavelength?

options.text: Speed decreases, frequency decreases, wavelength stays the same
Speed decreases, frequency stays the same, wavelength decreases
Speed increases, frequency stays the same, wavelength increases
Speed decreases, frequency stays the same, wavelength increases

questions.explanation: In shallow water, waves travel more slowly. The frequency is determined by the source and does not change when the medium changes. Since v = f x wavelength and f is constant while v decreases, the wavelength must also decrease. Option A incorrectly states frequency changes — frequency is always set by the source, not the medium.
